analysis.one_liner: Gives consumers one free credit score each year from every credit reporting agency, ending disclosure fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and died there when the Congress ended, despite 12 bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, you can already get a free copy of your credit report each year, but agencies could charge you for your credit score — the three-digit number lenders actually use to decide whether to lend to you and at what price. This bill would have required every nationwide credit reporting agency, including the specialty agencies that track medical payments, tenant and rental history, check writing, employment, and insurance claims, to give you one free credit score a year on request [S2][S3]. It repealed the existing fee provision for score disclosures [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers applying for mortgages, car loans, apartments, jobs, or insurance. People could check the score that decides their loan pricing and catch errors before they cost money, at no charge. Renters, job applicants, and people with thin credit files would gain visibility into the specialty files kept on them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and loan, rental, and job applicants

how_it_helps.text: Requires nationwide consumer reporting agencies to provide a free annual credit score disclosure upon consumer request, amending the Fair Credit Reporting Act [S2].
Extends the free disclosure to specialty agencies that compile medical records or payments, residential or tenant histories, check writing histories, employment histories, and insurance claims [S2].

Repeals the statutory provision (Section 609(f)(8) of FCRA) that allowed agencies to charge fees for credit score disclosures, except for fees the FTC determines fair and reasonable for disclosures beyond the free annual one [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus and credit score providers lose the revenue they earned selling credit scores directly to consumers. The FTC bears the cost of setting the 'fair and reasonable fee' standard for any non-free disclosures.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps the mandate at one free score per year per agency; consumers shopping for a mortgage across multiple lenders within a year could still be charged for additional scores, though any other fee would have to be 'fair and reasonable' as set by the FTC [S3].

A free score is not the same as a free mortgage score: the scores agencies disclose voluntarily can differ from the lender-specific versions used in underwriting, so the bill improves visibility but does not guarantee consumers see the exact score their lender uses.
Agencies could pass some compliance costs through in other products; the FTC would have to police 'fair and reasonable' fees, adding regulatory judgment calls [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: a free annual score is a small consumer win that lowers the cost of monitoring your own credit before a big purchase, and extending it to specialty files (rental, employment, insurance) helps people who are being judged on records they cannot see. The cost falls narrowly on credit bureaus' fee revenue. The bill would not have guaranteed access to the exact score a lender uses, so its practical value depended on which score agencies chose to disclose.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee the same day, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Udall of Colorado introduced the Fair Access to Credit Scores Act of 2010 on April 22, 2010, joined by nine original cosponsors from both parties [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever taken on the bill, and it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

The bill drew 12 cosponsors, including 4 of the Senate's 40 Republicans and 7 of 58 Democrats plus the chamber's lone Independent, giving it bipartisan support that never translated into committee action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies and credit score sellers are better off: they kept the right to charge consumers for their own credit scores for another two years, until free annual score disclosure was finally mandated by the 2013 amendment to the FCRA (effective 2015, via the Dodd-Frank rulemaking authority), which the industry had no reason to grant early. Consumers who paid for scores in the meantime were worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus, which kept score fees

for.name: Sen. Mark Udall
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; referred it to the Senate Banking Committee, where it stalled.

for.name: 12 cosponsors (4 of 40 Senate Republicans, 7 of 58 Senate Democrats, 1 of 1 Senate Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chairman, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, controlled the agenda and never brought the bill to a hearing or markup in the remaining months of the 111th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — 7 of 58 Senate Democrats, 4 of 40 Republicans, and the Senate's lone Independent signed on — so the bill did not die along party lines; it died from committee inaction.

industries.industry: Consumer credit reporting agencies and credit score providers
industries.note: The agencies (the big three bureaus and the specialty firms covering rental, employment, insurance, and medical files) had sold consumers their own scores and would have had to give one away free each year. Their interest in charging for scores ran directly against consumers' interest in seeing the number that prices their loans. (The industry side is inferred from the bill text's fee repeal; the congressional record does not document their lobbying.)
